extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, public law, and constitutional government
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate institutional criteria governing the relation between legislatures and executives (separation of powers, financial controls, discretion, vetoes, foreign affairs, parliamentary mechanisms) as described in a textbook account of national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of the purse as congressional control
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may check any particular scheme which the President favors by refusing supplies for it; withholding ordinary supplies would stop the machine of government but would injure the country and themselves more than the President. Congress cannot lawfully refuse the President's salary and cannot remove him except by successful impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Congress could withhold appropriations for military operations or purchase money for territory; but withholding supplies is self‑harmful and thus limited as an effective check. Practical limits on this power mean it is less effective than in many European countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of riders on appropriation bills
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of inserting provisions on quite different matters into money bills (''riders'') to coerce the President or pass measures otherwise difficult to enact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: 1867 (against Johnson) and 1879 (attempts against Hayes). Anti-patterns: tacking causes great abuses; many State constitutions forbid it. Contemporary remedy suggested: a constitutional amendment (line‑item veto) to allow vetoing single items without rejecting whole appropriation bills. House rule now declares an appropriation bill shall not carry any new legislation (not always strictly observed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers is difficult in theory and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although constitutions separate legislative, executive, and judicial departments, it is not easy to separate legislation and administration in analysis or to keep them apart in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook treats the practical overlap (e.g., legislature framing detailed laws that determine administrative action) and emphasizes examination of their relations in internal and foreign affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive discretion depends on particularity of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of an executive magistrate's power depends on how particular the law is: general laws leave wide discretion to the executive; minute, particular statutes narrow that discretion and reduce executive autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a general ad valorem duty leaves collection principles to the executive; a statute creating a post-office lets the executive fix rates. When law goes into minute details the executive 'becomes a mere servant' with little volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislatures tend to encroach on the executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Every legislature tends to enlarge its province and subject the executive to itself either by issuing decrees for particular cases or by framing laws so particular as to bind officials' discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resulting danger: absorption or extinction of the executive as an independent power, turning it into employees obeying the legislature. Historical parallels: ancient Greek assemblies, Roman practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms that protect the executive from legislative absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances that prevent the legislature from wholly absorbing the executive include allowing the executive to appeal to the nation (e.g., dissolution), popular support from reverence or military habit, and authority derived from foreign affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: England's power to dissolve Parliament; Prussia's stronger Crown with military influence; foreign policy importance gives executives discretionary authority that reacts to strengthen general executive weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary executive advantages: initiative, patronage, and dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: In parliamentary systems the executive/ministry retains practical advantages: initiative in legislation (sole in financial matters), patronage, control of parliamentary time, and the constitutional resource of dissolving Parliament to appeal to the electorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though legally dependent on Parliament, the ministry's organization and control of governmental business give it practical power; dissolution is a strategic resource that can succeed in securing public backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign affairs necessitate executive discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign policy cannot be provided for by general statutes in minute detail; it requires trained officials, promptness, and secrecy, so modern states leave foreign relations more to the executive than domestic affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the executive acquires wide discretion and influence in international matters; legislature's ability to regulate is limited by practical necessities of diplomacy and negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. constitutional compromise: independence of the President and veto power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution made the President independent of Congress (irremovable during term) and gave him a veto requiring a two‑thirds override, strengthening the President against legislative encroachment while at the same time limiting his initiative compared to a parliamentary executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founders feared an ambitious legislature and used the veto to give the executive negative legislative functions: he 'could not propose, but he could refuse.' This design both strengthens and weakens the President relative to parliamentary executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veto power as the executive's principal defensive strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The real strength of the executive in ordinary times is the veto power; the executive survives as an executive 'in virtue not of any properly executive function, but of the share in legislative functions which it has received.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experience: overrides are rare because two‑thirds majorities in both houses seldom align; thus the veto gives independence in practice even if constitutionally defeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative tools limit the President's constitutional functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many powers constitutionally incident to the executive (commander‑in‑chief, appointments, etc.) can be reached and constrained by statute (e.g., fixing army numbers, specifying qualifications, Senate confirmation, reducing salaries except for President and judges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: legislation can circumscribe executive reach; thus the President's formal constitutional powers may be practically limited by the 'long arm of legislation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power expands during emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: In moments of public danger (e.g., Civil War) the executive becomes immensely powerful because the legislature, recognizing its unfitness for swift and secret decisions, yields law‑making powers and practical authority to the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an accepted constitutional dynamic: emergency conditions temporarily rebalance power toward the executive for prompt action and defense.
